promptText: Why does reducing a model's numerical precision (quantization) not destroy its usefulness?
options: Because quantized models are always retrained from scratch at the new precision

Trained weights are highly redundant relative to the precision used to store them; what matters for a correct forward pass is each weight's approximate magnitude relative to other weights, not its exact value to many decimal places
Because inference never actually uses the weight values, only their sign
Because GPUs automatically upconvert INT4 values back to FP32 before every single operation, negating any precision loss
explanation: This is the foundational insight inherited from mobile/edge quantization: weights tolerate low precision because their approximate relative magnitude, not exact value, drives output.

promptText: What is the practical tradeoff of running a model via Ollama on local hardware versus calling a hosted API like OpenAI's?
options: Ollama guarantees strictly better output quality than any hosted API

Ollama removes per-token billing and network dependency and keeps data on your own hardware, but shifts responsibility for adequate memory/compute, quantization choice, and operating the serving process onto you
Hosted APIs cannot be used for any use case requiring data privacy
Ollama requires a GPU cluster and cannot run on a single machine
explanation: Self-hosting trades cost structure and control for operational responsibility that a hosted provider otherwise absorbs for you.

promptText: Between Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) and Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), which dominates practical local-deployment quantization, and why?
options: QAT dominates because it is cheaper and requires no training infrastructure

PTQ dominates because the whole point of self-hosting is usually to avoid running your own training infrastructure — you are shrinking an already-trained open-weight model, not training one from scratch; QAT is reserved for teams with the infrastructure and stakes to justify its extra cost
QAT dominates because it is required by every open-weight model license
PTQ and QAT are used with exactly equal frequency in practice
explanation: PTQ is cheap (minutes to hours, no retraining), matching the typical motivation for self-hosting; QAT is expensive and reserved for high-stakes deployments.

promptText: What is the core distinction between what GGUF/llama.cpp solved and what vLLM solved?
options: GGUF/llama.cpp made portable local inference possible (including CPU-only hardware); vLLM solved production-grade concurrent throughput via PagedAttention and continuous batching — they address different halves of the deployment problem
GGUF and vLLM both solve the exact same problem and are fully interchangeable
GGUF only works on GPUs; vLLM only works on CPUs
vLLM is a quantization format, while GGUF is a serving engine
explanation: GGUF/llama.cpp solved 'how do I run this at all' portably; vLLM solved 'how do I serve this to many concurrent users efficiently' — separate, complementary problems.

promptText: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric quantization?
options: Symmetric quantization is only used for activations; asymmetric only for weights

Symmetric quantization maps a float range centered on zero using a single scale factor with no zero-point offset; asymmetric quantization maps an arbitrary, possibly skewed range using both a scale and a zero-point offset, at the cost of a slightly more expensive dequantization step
Symmetric quantization always uses 8 bits; asymmetric always uses 4 bits
Asymmetric quantization cannot represent negative numbers
explanation: Symmetric is simpler and fits zero-centered weight distributions well; asymmetric handles skewed ranges (common in activations) more accurately using an added zero-point.

promptText: Why is per-channel or per-group quantization almost always more accurate than per-tensor quantization, especially at 4-bit?
options: Per-group quantization uses more bits per value than per-tensor quantization

Per-tensor quantization forces a single scale across the whole matrix, stretching precision to accommodate the tensor's largest outlier; per-group/per-channel quantization computes a separate scale for each smaller group, letting each group's scale fit its own actual value range
Per-tensor quantization is only compatible with FP32, not INT4
Per-group quantization eliminates the need for a zero-point entirely
explanation: Finer granularity avoids letting one outlier stretch the precision budget for an entire tensor, which is why GPTQ/AWQ configurations commonly use small group sizes.

promptText: How does GPTQ preserve more quality at 4-bit than simply rounding every weight independently and all at once?
options: GPTQ retrains the entire model from scratch at 4-bit precision using the calibration set as new training data

GPTQ quantizes one layer at a time using a calibration set, and after quantizing each column it corrects the remaining unquantized columns in that layer to compensate for the rounding error just introduced, so error is partially absorbed rather than compounding catastrophically
GPTQ only quantizes the first and last layers of the model, leaving the rest at full precision
GPTQ increases the model's parameter count to offset the precision loss
explanation: The layer-by-layer, error-correcting process is exactly why GPTQ preserves noticeably more quality at 4-bit than naive independent rounding of every weight.

promptText: What is the core mechanism AWQ uses to protect a small fraction of 'salient' weight channels from quantization error, without storing them at a different bit-width than the rest of the tensor?
options: AWQ deletes the salient channels entirely and reconstructs them at inference time using interpolation

AWQ scales the salient channels' weights up by a per-channel factor before quantization (reducing their relative rounding error) and divides the corresponding activations by the same factor at inference time to mathematically cancel the scaling out, protecting precision using ordinary uniform-precision storage
AWQ stores salient channels in FP32 while quantizing everything else to INT4, creating a mixed-precision tensor
AWQ identifies salient channels using a random sampling process unrelated to activation magnitude
explanation: AWQ finds channels with the largest activation magnitudes, protects them via a scale-before/undo-after trick, then quantizes uniformly — no mixed-precision storage needed.

promptText: Why does the chapter argue that KV cache memory, not weight memory, is frequently the binding constraint on how many concurrent users a self-hosted model can serve?
options: KV cache is always larger than the weight table regardless of concurrency or context length

KV cache size scales with the number of concurrent sequences and their context length, so serving even a modest number of concurrent long-context requests can require far more memory than the quantized weights themselves consume, a cost easy to underestimate if hardware is sized only against the weight table
KV cache memory is fixed at exactly 2GB regardless of model size or usage
Quantizing the weights automatically quantizes the KV cache to the same bit-width
explanation: KV cache scales roughly linearly with concurrent sequences and context length, and can dwarf weight memory the moment real concurrent traffic with long contexts arrives.

promptText: How does vLLM's combination of PagedAttention and continuous batching increase throughput compared to a naive request-at-a-time server?
options: It increases throughput by always running requests with the largest possible batch size regardless of memory usage

PagedAttention allocates each request's KV cache in fixed-size, non-contiguous pages instead of one large reserved block, avoiding fragmentation waste; continuous batching admits new requests and evicts completed ones on every generation step instead of waiting for a whole fixed batch to finish together
It increases throughput by converting all requests to INT4 precision automatically before serving
It increases throughput solely by using a faster network protocol between client and server
explanation: PagedAttention manages the KV cache like OS virtual memory, and continuous batching keeps the GPU busy by admitting/evicting requests per step rather than per whole batch.

promptText: The chapter frames self-hosting as decomposing into a 'compression failure' and a 'serving failure.' Why does conflating the two waste engineering effort?
options: Because compression and serving failures always have the same root cause, so distinguishing them is meaningless

A team might spend a sprint chasing ever-more-aggressive quantization to fix what is actually a serving-configuration problem (e.g., under-provisioned KV cache or batch sizing), or rewrite serving infrastructure to fix a genuine quality regression that only a less aggressive quantization setting could repair
Compression failures can only be diagnosed by the model vendor, never by the deploying team
Serving failures never occur once a model has been successfully quantized
explanation: Diagnosing which half broke, by checking evaluation scores and serving-stack saturation independently, is the entire practical payoff of treating this as two separable problems.

promptText: The chapter shows that for the same weight range, an INT4 bucket is roughly 16x wider than the corresponding INT8 bucket. Why does this specifically necessitate GPTQ/AWQ-style error correction at 4-bit rather than naive independent rounding, when INT8 often tolerates naive rounding reasonably well?
options: INT4 buckets are actually narrower than INT8 buckets, so the premise is false

A much wider bucket means each individual weight's rounding error is proportionally far larger relative to the tensor's value range; at that error magnitude, uncorrected, independent rounding across many weights introduces enough aggregate distortion to measurably harm output quality, whereas calibrated layer-wise correction (GPTQ) or protecting salient channels (AWQ) actively compensates for or minimizes that larger error
INT4 requires error correction only because it is incompatible with symmetric quantization
Error correction is needed at INT4 because GPUs cannot perform INT4 arithmetic natively, unlike INT8
explanation: The 16x wider bucket at INT4 makes uncorrected rounding error large enough to measurably harm quality, which is exactly why calibrated techniques become necessary rather than optional.

promptText: For a 7B-class model (32 layers, 32 heads, head_dim 128) at FP16 KV cache, 4096 context, batch size 1, the chapter computes roughly 2 GiB of KV cache per sequence — so 16 concurrent sequences need roughly 32 GiB of KV cache alone. Why can this make INT4 weight quantization's memory savings almost irrelevant at moderate concurrency?
options: Because KV cache is always quantized identically to the weights, so any weight savings pass through unchanged

Because dropping weights from 14GB (FP16) to 3.5GB (INT4) saves roughly 10.5GB, but 16 concurrent long-context sequences alone can require ~32GB of KV cache — a cost driven by concurrency and context length, not weight precision — so the weight-side savings can be dwarfed by an under-provisioned KV cache budget
Because KV cache scales down automatically whenever weights are quantized to a lower bit-width
Because INT4 quantization eliminates the need for a KV cache entirely
explanation: The KV cache cost is orthogonal to weight precision and grows with concurrency and context length, so it can easily exceed the entire memory savings gained from aggressive weight quantization.

promptText: Self-hosting shifts certain security responsibilities from a hosted provider onto the deploying team. Which pair of risks does the chapter identify as genuine (not theoretical) concerns specific to local deployment?
options: Risk of GPU overheating and risk of running out of disk space — both purely hardware maintenance issues unrelated to security

Model file supply-chain risk (some serialization formats like raw Python pickle allow arbitrary code execution on load, so an untrusted downloaded checkpoint can compromise the host) and unauthenticated local inference endpoints (Ollama/vLLM's OpenAI-compatible servers do not enforce authentication or rate-limiting by default, so exposing one on a reachable network interface hands anyone unmetered access to the model and GPU budget)
Risk of the model refusing to answer questions and risk of the model being too slow — both purely performance issues
Risk of losing internet connectivity and risk of running out of RAM — both purely availability issues with no security dimension
explanation: A hosted provider absorbs authentication, rate-limiting, and artifact provenance for you; self-hosting makes both model supply-chain integrity and endpoint access control the deploying team's job.

promptText: Per the chapter's decision tree, when should a team choose vLLM over Ollama or llama.cpp, and why is the quantization format (GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ) considered a separate decision axis from the serving-stack choice?
options: vLLM should always be chosen because it is the newest tool; format and serving stack are the same decision because GGUF only works with vLLM

vLLM is the right choice when serving many concurrent production users with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, continuous batching, and efficient KV cache use; format is separate from serving stack because GGUF works with Ollama/llama.cpp while vLLM consumes GPTQ/AWQ checkpoints directly — assuming a format locks you into one specific server is a common, avoidable confusion
vLLM should only be used for CPU-only deployments with no GPU available
Ollama and vLLM require completely different, mutually incompatible quantization formats, so the choice must be made before any quantization work begins
explanation: Serving-stack choice and quantization-format choice are largely independent axes; conflating them, as in 'we have to use Ollama because we quantized with GPTQ,' is a common avoidable mistake.
